procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated December 3, 1968, of the Delhi High Court in Civil Writ Petition No. 817 of 1968.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: Appellants filed a writ petition challenging the power of the Central Government to make nominations for admissions to Maulana Azad Medical College. The High Court dismissed the petition on December 3, 1968. Appellants then filed a review petition under s. 114 and 0. 47, R. I read with s. 141, Civil Procedure Code, which was dismissed by the High Court on January 27, 1969.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: Appellants sought leave to appeal to the Supreme Court against both the judgment dismissing the writ petition and the order dismissing the review petition. However, the certificate granted by the High Court only mentioned the judgment dated December 3, 1968. The Supreme Court noted that an order rejecting a review application is not appealable under 0. 47, R. 7, and the appellants did not seek leave to appeal under Art. 136. Therefore, the arguments were confined to the matters decided by the judgment dated December 3, 1968. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal.

issue.issue_text: Whether an order rejecting an application for review under Order 47, Rule 7 of the Civil Procedure Code is appealable in the normal course.

facts: The appellants filed a petition to review a High Court judgment.
The High Court dismissed the review petition by an order dated January 27, 1969.
The appellants then sought leave to appeal to the Supreme Court against both the original judgment and the order dismissing the review petition.
The certificate granted by the High Court for the appeal was limited only to the original judgment, not the order dismissing the review.
law: Under Order 47, Rule 7 of the Civil Procedure Code, an order of a court rejecting an application for review is not appealable.
The proper way to challenge an order rejecting a review petition before the Supreme Court is by seeking special leave to appeal under Article 136 of the Constitution.
application: The Supreme Court noted that the High Court's certificate was correctly limited to the appeal against the original judgment.
The Court reasoned that this was because the order rejecting the review application is explicitly made non-appealable by Order 47, Rule 7.
The Court further observed that the appellants had not sought the alternative remedy of asking for special leave under Article 136 to challenge the dismissal of the review.
As a result, the Court only considered arguments related to the original judgment and not the order dismissing the review.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that an order rejecting an application for review is not appealable in the normal course, based on the express prohibition contained in Order 47, Rule 7 of the Civil Procedure Code.

issue.issue_text: Whether appellants who do not compete for reserved seats have the locus standi to challenge the nominations made by the Central Government to such seats.

facts: Appellants applied for admission to general, non-reserved seats in a medical college but were not admitted.
They challenged the nominations made by the Central Government to a separate category of reserved seats.

The appellants argued that if the nominations to the reserved seats were found to be improper, those seats should be made available to the general pool of candidates, which would give them a chance at admission.
law: The legal principle of 'locus standi' requires a person bringing a legal action to have a sufficient connection to and harm from the law or action they are challenging. In other words, they must have a right or interest in the matter.
application: The Supreme Court reasoned that the appellants did not compete for the reserved seats in question.
Because they were not candidates for the reserved seats, the Court found they had no legal right or standing ('locus standi') to challenge the nominations made to those specific seats.
The Court explicitly rejected the appellants' assumption that improperly filled reserved seats would automatically be transferred to the general pool.

It clarified that the Central Government was under no obligation to release those seats to the general pool and could not be compelled to do so at the request of students from the non-reserved category.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that the appellants did not have the locus standi (the right or standing) to challenge the nominations to the reserved seats because they did not compete for those seats and had no legal claim to them, even if the nominations were found to be invalid.

issue.issue_text: Whether reserved seats that are not properly filled up according to the rules must be converted and thrown open to the general pool.

facts: Appellants, who were candidates for the general pool of seats, challenged the nominations made by the Central Government to reserved seats.
They argued that if the nominations to reserved seats were not made in accordance with the rules, those seats should be considered improperly filled.
The appellants contended that these improperly filled reserved seats should then be converted and made available to the general pool, for which they were competing.
law: Candidates who do not compete for reserved seats have no legal standing ('locus standi') to challenge the nominations made to those seats.
There is no rule or obligation that compels the government to convert improperly filled reserved seats into general pool seats.
The government has the discretion to release reserved seats to the general pool in the larger interest of other candidates, but it cannot be forced to do so.
application: The Supreme Court first determined that the appellants, as general pool candidates, had no right or 'locus standi' to challenge the nominations for the reserved seats since they were not in competition for them.
The Court then directly addressed the appellants' main argument, calling the assumption that improperly filled reserved seats would be thrown open to the general pool "wholly unfounded."
It clarified that the Central Government is under "no obligation" to release those seats to the general pool.
While acknowledging that the government *could* release the seats, the Court emphasized that it "cannot be compelled to do so" at the request of students from the general category.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument, concluding that the idea that improperly filled reserved seats must be converted to the general pool was "wholly unfounded." The Court held that the government has no obligation to release such seats to the general pool, and candidates from the general pool have no right to demand it.

issue.issue_text: Whether it is for the courts to interfere with the manner and method of making a reasonable classification of seats, such as on a territorial or geographical basis.

facts: A centrally administered medical college reserved seats for specific categories of students, including those from certain geographical areas like Union territories other than Delhi.
The appellants, who were denied admission, challenged this reservation, arguing that the classification was unreasonable and violated the Constitution.
The method for filling these reserved seats was nomination by the Central Government, which was also challenged as discriminatory.
law: The Court reiterated the principle that Article 14 of the Constitution forbids class legislation but permits reasonable classification.

A permissible classification must be founded on an intelligible differentia that distinguishes the grouped individuals from others, and this differentia must have a rational relation to the objective.
The Court distinguished this case from precedents like *Minor P. Rajendran*, where a district-wise classification was struck down because it lacked a reasonable relation to the objective.
application: The Court found that the classification of seats on a geographical basis for residents of Union territories was reasonable. It reasoned that these areas were comparatively backward and, for the most part, did not have their own medical colleges, thus justifying the need to provide them with educational facilities.

The Court also found the method of nomination by the Central Government to be appropriate. It reasoned that since candidates for reserved seats were drawn from diverse sources with different educational backgrounds and examination standards, the Central Government was the most suitable authority to make a proper selection.

The Court held that since the underlying classification was reasonable, the specific manner and method of implementing it (i.e., nomination by the government) was not a matter for judicial interference.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that once a classification of seats, whether on a territorial, geographical, or other basis, is found to be reasonable, it is not for the courts to interfere with the manner and method of making that classification. Therefore, the challenge was rejected.

arguments.issue_text: Whether an order rejecting an application for review under Order 47, Rule 7 of the Civil Procedure Code is appealable in the normal course.
appellant_arguments: The appellants sought leave to appeal against the order by which their review petition was disposed of, implying they believed it was appealable.
respondent_arguments: An order rejecting an application for review is not appealable under Order 47, Rule 7 of the Civil Procedure Code.

arguments.issue_text: Whether appellants who do not compete for reserved seats have the locus standi to challenge the nominations made by the Central Government to such seats.
appellant_arguments: The appellants had the right to challenge the nominations made by the Central Government to the reserved seats.
The nominations to the reserved seats were contrary to the rules.
respondent_arguments: The appellants did not compete for the reserved seats and therefore had no locus standi (right to bring an action) to challenge the nominations for those seats.

arguments.issue_text: Whether reserved seats that are not properly filled up according to the rules must be converted and thrown open to the general pool.
appellant_arguments: If nominations to reserved seats were not in accordance with the rules, such seats must be considered not properly filled and should be thrown open to the general pool of candidates.
respondent_arguments: The Central Government is under no obligation to release improperly filled reserved seats to the general pool and cannot be compelled to do so.

arguments.issue_text: Whether it is for the courts to interfere with the manner and method of making a reasonable classification of seats, such as on a territorial or geographical basis.
appellant_arguments: The rules for reservation of seats were not based on any reasonable classification and were therefore violative of Article 14 of the Constitution.
The rules also violated clauses (1) and (4) of Article 15 and clause (2) of Article 29 of the Constitution.
respondent_arguments: The classification of seats was reasonable and not violative of the Constitution.

cases.case_name: Shri Ram Krishna Dalmia v. Shri Justice S. R. Tendolkar & Others
cases.principle: Article 14 forbids class legislation but not reasonable classification. For a classification to be permissible, it must fulfill two conditions: (i) it must be founded on an intelligible differentia which distinguishes persons or things that are grouped together from others left out of the group, and (ii) the differentia must have a rational relation to the object sought to be achieved.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A person who does not compete for reserved seats has no legal standing (locus standi) to challenge the nominations made to those seats. Furthermore, if a nomination to a reserved seat is not made in accordance with the rules, the government is under no legal obligation to release that seat to the general pool of candidates. When a classification for reservation is made on a territorial, geographical, or other reasonable basis, it is not for the courts to interfere with the manner and method of making that classification.
obiter: The High Court was in error in going into the question and holding that some seats filled by nomination had been filled contrary to the admission rules and would be converted into the general pool.
The Central Government may, in the larger interest of giving maximum benefit to candidates belonging to the non-reserved seats, release some reserved seats, but it cannot be compelled to do so.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Central Government, which bears the financial burden of running the medical college, has the right to lay down the criteria for eligibility and decide from what sources admissions will be made. This is essentially a question of policy. If the sources for admission are properly classified on a territorial, geographical, or other reasonable basis, it is not for the courts to interfere with the manner and method of making that classification. Furthermore, individuals who do not compete for reserved seats have no locus standi to challenge the nominations made to those seats.
legal_tests_applied: To pass the test of permissible classification under Article 14, two conditions must be fulfilled: (i) that the classification is founded on intelligible differentia which distinguishes persons or things that are grouped together from others left out of the group and, (ii) that that differentia must have a rational relation to the object sought to be achieved.
why_appellant_lost: The appellants did not have any right to challenge the nominations made by the Central Government. They did not compete for the reserved seats and had no locus standi in the matter of nomination to such seats.

The contention that if nominations to reserved seats were not in accordance with the rules, such seats must be regarded as not having been properly filled and must be thrown open to the general pool, was wholly unfounded. The Central Government was under no obligation to release those seats to the general pool.
The rules do not discriminate between any citizen on grounds only of religion, race, caste, sex, place of birth or any of them, and therefore Article 15(1) cannot be invoked.

The appellants were not being denied admission into the Medical College on grounds only of religion, race, caste, language, sex or place of birth, and therefore Article 29(2) was of no assistance to them.
why_respondent_won: The classification of seats was based on an intelligible differentia which distinguishes the reserved groups from the group to which the appellants belong. The reserved categories included residents of comparatively backward Union territories without medical colleges, children of Central Government servants posted abroad facing educational difficulties, scholars under reciprocal arrangements, and scholars from Jammu & Kashmir which has peculiar problems and inadequate medical education arrangements.

The classification has a rational nexus with the object of imparting medical education, as the authorities who run the institution have the right to determine the sources from which students are to be drawn.
It is for the Central Government, which bears the financial burden of running the medical college, to lay down the criteria for eligibility and decide from what sources the admission will be made.
policy_considerations: The Government cannot be denied the right to decide from what sources the admission will be made. That essentially is a question of policy and depends inter-alia on an overall assessment and survey of the requirements of residents of particular territories and other categories of persons for whom it is essential to provide facilities for medical education.
If the sources are properly classified whether on territorial, geographical or other reasonable basis it is not for the courts to interfere with the manner and method of making the classification.
